questions.problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2xy-1}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1) & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}(2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot (2x\cdot 1-0) \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{\sqrt{2xy-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}y,$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+{x}^{2}\cdot (1) \\  & =x{e}^{xy}\cdot (1)+{x}^{2} \\  & =x{e}^{xy}+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}+{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y\cdot (1) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},2) & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {2}^{2}+2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot 2) \\  & =2\pi +2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =2\pi +2\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+1)^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1) & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (1+0) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}y}\cdot y\cdot 2x-y\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(2,\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) & =x(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y))+\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =x(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-y\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi )} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(-1-\pi \cdot 0)+(-1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(2,\sqrt{5}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain, the sum, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) & =1\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot 0+2y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\sqrt{5}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\sqrt{5})} & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}+\frac{{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+5}+\frac{5}{\sqrt{4+5}} \\  & =3+\frac{5}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) & =(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}))-{x}^{2}\cdot (2y) \\  & =(1\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot 1)-2{x}^{2}y \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}-2{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,1)} & ={e}^{1\cdot 1}+1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 1}-2\cdot {1}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =e+e-2 \\  & =2e-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)))+\sqrt{y}\cdot (1) \\  & =(1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1+\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1/4,4)} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4)+1+\sqrt{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ for $f(x,y)={x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x{y}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{y}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{y}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))-{y}^{3}\cdot (1) \\  & =((4{x}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{4}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x))-{y}^{3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-{x}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot (y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(0,2)} & =\frac{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡0-0\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2+0}{(2+0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y}{{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{{sin}^{2}⁡y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,\pi /2)} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(\pi +\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1-0}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2x{y}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}y}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2h(x,y)}{{x}^{3}y}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{2x{y}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}y}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot {x}^{2}y-(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)}{({x}^{2}y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{y}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}y-(2x{y}^{2}-1)\cdot 2xy}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-4{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2xy}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy-2{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy(1-x{y}^{2})}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-x{y}^{2})}{{x}^{3}y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
h(x,y)=1-x{y}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x+y)\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x+y})}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y))}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot 1)}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6(x+y)-(3x+y)}{2\sqrt{x+y}})}{x+y} \\  & =\frac{3x+5y}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=3x+5y.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{x-{y}^{2}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{x-{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (x-{y}^{2})-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x-{y}^{2})}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2y\cdot (x-{y}^{2})-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (-2y)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy-2{y}^{3}+2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy+2{x}^{2}y}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2xy(1+x)}{{(x-{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=2xy(1+x).
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(3,-1,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({({x}^{2}+4{z}^{2})}^{1/2}) \\  & =y\cdot (\frac{1}{2}{({x}^{2}+4{z}^{2})}^{-1/2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{z}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}) & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\cdot (2x+0) \\  & =\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,-1,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(3,-1,-2)} & =\frac{(3)(-1)}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+4(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{9+16}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{25}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(1,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-(0) \\  & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2y) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2(1)^{2}(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xyz-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,0,\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz\cdot 1-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) \\  & =yz-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}yz-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz)) & =yz-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xz) \\  & =yz-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz)\cdot (z) \\  & =yz-z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz) \\  & =z(y-\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,0,\pi )} & =\pi (0-\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )) \\  & =\pi (0-(-1)) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}{e}^{xy}-{y}^{2}{e}^{yz},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy}-{y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz}) & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot y \\  & =2z{e}^{xy}-{y}^{3}{e}^{yz}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}{|}_{(0,-1,1)} & =2(1){e}^{(0)(-1)}-(-1)^{3}{e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =2+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)$ for $g(x,y,z)=(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z+(z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z+(z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}((z+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =(x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z+y) \\  & =(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot 1 \\  & =(x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡z+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{4x-y}{x+y^2},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(2,-1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4x-y}{x+{y}^{2}}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2})}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot 1}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4x+4{y}^{2}-4x+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{y}^{2}+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,-1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(2,-1)} & =\frac{4(-1)^{2}+(-1)}{{(2+{(-1)}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function  $g(x,y,z) = 2 (x + 1)e^z+ yz,$  evaluate  $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}$ at $(1,1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z}+yz) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1)\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1){e}^{z}+y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(1,1,1)} & =2(1+1){e}^{1}+1 \\  & =4e+1\end{aligned}
$$
